title: Tamsin and the House
premise: Rafael Nystrom, a pest controller with a habit of counting doors and keeping lights burning, is called to Tamsin House, where something leaves fingerprints on the inside of sealed windows. When the village church bell rings — a bell melted down in 1911 — Rafael and the house's last heir are pulled into a night that will not end until sunrise. To survive, they must uncover what the house's original owners invited in through the well before it refills at dawn. Rafael holds the door until sunrise, but belonging to the house means one of them must stay behind as its new memory.
about_author: Emrys Delacroix is the pen name of a former rural surveyor who spent years cataloguing abandoned properties across northern England. Their fiction draws on field notes, parish records, and the particular silence of houses that have outlived their owners.

chapters.title: The Call-Out
chapters.summary: Rafael Nystrom's POV. A routine pest-control call to derelict Tamsin House turns strange: droppings that aren't droppings, and fingerprints on the inside of boarded windows. Rafael's professional calm masks unease; the emotional beat is the first crack in rationality.

chapters.title: Fingerprints on the Glass
chapters.summary: Rafael returns for equipment left behind and finds every door open except the ones he counted shut. The heir, Maren Tamsin, arrives claiming she never called anyone. POV alternates; the beat is wary alliance between two strangers who both feel watched.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: In the village, the church bell rings at midnight though it was melted down in 1911. Villagers deny hearing it. Rafael and Maren, standing in the churchyard, are suddenly pulled — mid-step — back into the house's great hall. Beat: reality's rules break.

chapters.title: Doors and Lights
chapters.summary: Trapped in a looping night, Rafael does what he knows: counts doors, keeps lights on. The count changes each circuit — eleven doors, then twelve. Maren finds her grandmother's diary. Beat: ritual and routine as armor against dread.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Wrote
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The diary reveals the 1911 bell was sold to fund a sealing of the well after something was 'invited in' during a harvest rite. The fingerprints belong to the invited thing wearing the family's hands. Beat: inheritance revealed as debt.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: Water sounds rise from beneath the kitchen floor. The house's rooms rearrange around the sound of filling. Rafael realizes sunrise won't come until the well is full — or answered. Beat: the deadline becomes physical, rising like water.

chapters.title: The Invited Guest
chapters.summary: The entity manifests using the faces of every Tamsin who ever welcomed it, asking each generation the same question: do you belong here? Maren nearly answers yes. Rafael drags her back. Beat: temptation of belonging at any cost.

chapters.title: Parish Records
chapters.summary: Maren finds the rite's terms in the vestry minutes: the invitation can be refused by an heir who gives up claim to the house entirely. But refusal strands whoever else is inside. Beat: the cost of escape made explicit.

chapters.title: Sunrise Terms
chapters.summary: Climax. As water reaches the floorboards, Maren refuses the inheritance aloud — but the house takes Rafael instead, the one who kept its lights on and counted its doors, who belonged without blood. He holds the final door against the well's overflow until dawn breaks.

chapters.title: The New Memory
chapters.summary: Resolution, Maren's POV. Sunrise comes; the village bell is silent stone. Maren visits yearly, leaving lights on out of guilt and love. In the windows, sometimes, fresh fingerprints appear on the inside — patient, familiar, counting doors of its own.
